header:
Date: 2026-05-20
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen, Liam O'Connor, Sofia Reyes (Redwood) — Priya Patel, Daniel Ruiz, Ellen Cho, Mark Benson, Asha Verma (Greenlane)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll give folks a minute to hop in. hey Priya?
[00:12] Priya Patel: here, thanks Maya. morning team. quick one — we had a couple of late folks so no worries.
[00:20] Liam O'Connor: hi, Liam from Redwood, I'll lead the tuning bits today and run through the sizing sheet.
[00:28] Daniel Ruiz: Daniel, SRE. saw some noise in logs this morning during the simulated surge, p99 spiked.
[00:35] Maya Chen: quick agenda — 1) quick readout of week 3 metrics 2) autoscale and burst policy proposals 3) KV-prefix caching and prompt hotspots 4) runbook for the rehearsal 5) next steps. sound good?
[00:45] Ellen Cho: yep, yep good.
[01:05] Liam O'Connor: okay reading the metrics — so in the synthetic 2x surge we ran on Tuesday we saw median latency about 120ms, p95 at 340ms, p99 at 1.2s which is higher than expected. notable is variance across replicas; eu-west nodes had slightly higher tail. we suspect cold-start + context-window overhead for long prompts.
[01:38] Priya Patel: that p99 is the one that worries us — our SLO target is 500ms p95 and we want p99 under 800ms ideally. we hit p95 sometimes but p99 is the outlier.
[01:52] Sofia Reyes: a couple of quick clarifications — when you say long prompts, what's the typical seq len distribution? are these customer prompts or system-primed templates?
[02:05] Mark Benson: mostly system priming + diagnostic attachments, about 512 tokens average but the burst traffic included some 1k token requests.
[02:15] Liam O'Connor: that helps. longer sequence lengths increase KV footprint and memory pressure on GPUs; that explains the variance across replicas. also noticed request distribution was bursty — many concurrent cold sessions at once.
[02:36] Daniel Ruiz: we saw some queueing in the worker pods too, the autoscaler seemed slow to add replicas for the peak. policy was conservative — scale up threshold at 70% GPU util and cool-down 3 minutes.
[02:50] Maya Chen: right that's one of the policy knobs we want to adjust. Liam, what are the recommended policy changes?
[02:58] Liam O'Connor: recommended changes: drop scale-up threshold to 55% for burst hours, decrease cool-down to 60s, and add a pre-warming burst pool (reserved nodes) for the expected 10-minute peaks. additionally, set a faster fallback to lower-cost model variant when tail latency > 900ms to keep end-user experience.
[03:20] Ellen Cho: tell me more about the fallback to lower-cost model — will that change output quality?
[03:26] Liam O'Connor: yes there is a tradeoff. Redwood supports model variants in the catalog — a quantized variant with 7B quantization does reduce latency significantly but might alter generation style slightly. the idea is to only fall back for short windows to avoid complete outage. we can A/B that in rehearsal.
[03:48] Priya Patel: could we route only non-critical traffic to the fallback? i.e., non-SLA customer flows or background jobs?
[03:56] Sofia Reyes: absolutely, routing policies can be request-tag-aware — prefix or header flags, even per-API-key routing. that way we keep critical user flows on the primary path.
[04:10] Daniel Ruiz: we want to avoid surprises. how do we detect the <900ms threshold automatically? is that in the observations from the console or do we ingest metrics elsewhere?
[04:20] Liam O'Connor: Redwood Console emits token-level latency metrics and a p99 alert stream; you can configure a short-window evaluation rule — e.g., if p99 > 900ms for two evaluation windows (1 min windows) trigger fallback. that'll be in the rollout policy object.
[04:36] Mark Benson: and what about cold-starts? we saw a couple of 2s responses early in the test.
[04:42] Sofia Reyes: those were cold-kernel paths, yes. adding pre-warm nodes reduces cold starts. also KV caching for repeated prompt prefixes will avoid cost of re-encoding common system messages.
[04:55] Priya Patel: about KV-prefix caching — can you explain implementation and invalidation? we have quite a few dynamic system prompts.
[05:05] Sofia Reyes: sure — you identify hot prefix tokens (like system priming or common instruction blocks). at the runtime level we persist KV caches on the serving node for those prefix sequences; next requests with the same prefix reuse the KV and skip recomputation. invalidation options: TTL or event-driven flush (via API) when you update templates. it's not instantaneous but we recommend TTL of 15-30 minutes for most cases.
[05:30] Daniel Ruiz: does that change memory footprint a lot? we're already memory constrained on the smaller GPUs.
[05:36] Liam O'Connor: some increase, but it's more efficient than recomputing encodings repeatedly. also, if memory pressure is high, the runtime will evict least recently used prefixes. For the DGX-style GPUs we saw about 8-12% increase in memory usage for typical prefix sets.
[05:52] Ellen Cho: let's talk sizing — Liam you mentioned a spreadsheet. what's the recommended GPU mix for our baseline vs burst?
[06:00] Liam O'Connor: baseline using A100-style instances we recommend a pool of 6 GPUs for steady state (handles median load with room for 30% headroom). For burst we recommend a reserved burst pool of 3 additional GPUs with faster scale-up policy; or if you want lower-cost, mix in 4x T4/RTX 6000 equivalent for non-critical fallback workload. I'll send the per-region per-model sheet.
[06:23] Priya Patel: EU region had worse tails — is that network or infra?
[06:29] Liam O'Connor: initial signals point to warm-up sequencing and slightly higher request coalescing times; also the EU test ran against a slightly older model checkpoint we had pinned. We recommend aligning model version across regions and applying the same quantization profile to ensure parity.
[06:48] Mark Benson: about model pinning — how do rollouts work for pinned versions? can we do canary in EU only?
[06:55] Sofia Reyes: yes, rollouts are per-region or per-route. you can pin traffic percentages by API key or region and do a canary for 5–10% before full rollout. fallback policies remain active during rollout.
[07:10] Priya Patel: compliance question — data residency and logs. Asha, any concerns?
[07:15] Asha Verma: yes, SOC2 controls are fine but we need audit log retention and KMS key separation for EU data. do you support customer-managed keys for Private?
[07:26] Maya Chen: yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and separate audit retention. for Hosted we offer region-restricted storage and encryption at rest, but customer-managed KMS is only on Private or Dedicated with an enterprise contract.
[07:45] Asha Verma: ok we'll flag that as an ask.
[07:50] Daniel Ruiz: about the rehearsal — what traffic shapes should we run? the 2x was useful but we need a longer sustained spike.
[07:58] Liam O'Connor: propose a 6-hour rehearsal: start with ramp to 2x over 10 minutes, hold 1 hour, spike to 5x for 15 minutes repeated 3 times over the 6 hours, include a long sequence (1k tokens) mix at 20% of requests. we'll also run background low-priority queries to validate fallback routing.
[08:22] Priya Patel: that seems right. can Redwood simulate from eu-west to validate network topology?
[08:29] Liam O'Connor: yes we can generate traffic from eu-west and us-east. We'll provide the exact load generator script and parameters.
[08:36] Mark Benson: monitoring — will we get corpus-level quality checks during fallback? we can't have hallucination regressions.
[08:44] Sofia Reyes: we can hook in eval sets and run lightweight quality checks on the output; Redwood Optimize has an eval runner that can score outputs during rehearsal and flag quality delta over threshold. we'll surface that in Console with diff views.
[09:00] Ellen Cho: minimal acceptable quality delta?
[09:03] Liam O'Connor: usually teams set a 3–5% drop tolerance for fallback windows depending on criticality. If above 5% then we recommend aborting the fallback and trying alternate routing.
[09:15] Daniel Ruiz: one more item — autoscaler observed slow scale-downs which contributed to oscillation. suggestions?
[09:21] Liam O'Connor: for scale-down, add a hysteresis period and use a step-down policy to reduce one replica at a time with a longer cool-down (5–10 min) to avoid oscillation. Also use amortized CPU/GPU util metrics rather than instantaneous to smooth signals.
[09:38] Priya Patel: any notes on cost? we need a rough monthly delta if we add reserved burst capacity vs relying on on-demand.
[09:45] Liam O'Connor: rough numbers: reserved pool reduces per-token cost by ~18% compared to on-demand burst. I'll put actuals in the sizing spreadsheet with both on-demand and reserved options and cost-neutral breakpoints.
[09:58] Maya Chen: quick check — are there competitor concerns to call out?
[10:02] Ellen Cho: we had a procurement ask to compare to Anthropic on quality and OpenAI on latency for short prompts. but our main requirement is predictability and auditability so pricing plus Private options are key.
[10:15] Maya Chen: noted. we'll include a short matrix in the workbook.
[10:20] Sofia Reyes: action item recap: I'll send KV prefix config examples; Liam will send sizing workbook; Maya will share rehearsal window options; Redwood will run initial EU simulation.
[10:35] Priya Patel: timeline-wise can we aim to lock the rehearsal for 2026-05-28?
[10:40] Maya Chen: yes we're targeting that, pending your confirmation of traffic shape by Monday 2026-05-24.
[10:48] Daniel Ruiz: we'll run our internal generator and share the shape and list of hot prompts by 2026-05-24.
[10:55] Asha Verma: on SOC2 gaps I'll loop in legal and return with questions by next Tuesday.
[11:05] Ellen Cho: sounds good. also please mark any known fallout scenarios in the runbook — e.g., region failover and model rollback steps.
[11:12] Sofia Reyes: we'll add explicit rollback steps and a playbook for circuit-breaker behavior.
[11:20] Maya Chen: any other blockers?
[11:24] Mark Benson: none from product.
[11:26] Priya Patel: all good.
[11:30] Maya Chen: great, thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email with the attachments.
[11:36] END OF TRANSCRIPT: meeting closed and recording stopped.
questions: What autoscale thresholds should we use for burst hours?
How will KV-prefix caching affect memory and eviction?
Can we route non-critical traffic to a quantized fallback variant during spikes?
Do you support customer-managed KMS for Dedicated/Private?
What traffic shape will Redwood simulate for the EU rehearsal?
